text:
Using trout habitat boundaries of 20 C. and 4.0 mg/l, Applicant has shown that trout habitat in the Whitewater Arm of Lake Jocassee went from 9.0 meters in thickness to 2.5 meters in thickness during the summer of 1974. During the same period, habitat was reduced from 25 meters to 19 meters in thickness in the main body of the reservoir. Cove and tributary arms would contain less trout habitat during the summer. As habitat is lost during the late summer, trout could move out of these regions and into portions of the lake containing more habitat. Due to inflows and variations in stratification, there may be some areas that would maintain suitable trout water throughout the summer.
Comparison of the data during the stratified periods of 1973 through 1975 shows a decrease in the size of the available trout habitat in Lake Jocassee (Figure 2-22). While data for 1973 are included in this figure, it should be noted that Lake Jocassee was not completely full during this year. In March of 1973, Lake Jocassee was about 17.5 meters (57.3 feet) below full pool elevation of 1,110 feet msl. In June, the lake was 8.5 meters (28 feet) below full pool and in September, 5.3 meters (17.3 feet) below elevation 1,110. Thus, during the beginning of the warming period, Lake Jocassee contained only about 68 percent of the total capacity, with in excess of 350,000 acre-feet of volume remaining to be filled. Therefore, any conclusions regarding changes in trout habitat from 1973 should be made with caution.
While the data show a reduction in the thickness of the trout habitat in Lake Jocassee from 1974 to 1975, the reduction in the volume of water in the trout habitat is of more significance. SERI has made preliminary estimates of the volumes of the trout water band by an assumed prorating of percent of Lake Jocassee represented by each of their sampling stations. Their analysis shows a reduction in trout habitat from 355,493 acre-feet in August 1974 to 294,978 acre-feet in August 1975 (assuming trout habitat boundaries of 20 C and 5.0 mg/l DO). For September, the reduction is from 221,241 acre-feet in 1974 to 126,113 acrefeet in 1975 (Table 2-10). Similar decreases, but of somewhat lesser magnitude, were calculated using habitat boundaries of 21 C and 3.0 mg/l. This reduction in volume of trout. habitat could ultimately lead to crowding of trout and a reduction in the carrying capacity of the Lake for trout. Given the stocking rate and size of Lake Jocassee, this would not be expected to be a problem at present.
